scripts.title: The typo test
scripts.note: Top performer: 3 likes, 1 comment, 53 reach (Oct 12 card). Warm-up take, record it first. Hold the phone up on 'grab your phone'.
scripts.source: IG card 2026-10-12 https://www.instagram.com/p/DeZ4YUNHAtG/ · Search Engine Roundtable, Oct 12 2026
scripts.script:
Spell your business name wrong on Google.
Go ahead… your customers will.

Search Engine Roundtable reported that Google's AI Overviews often show up when a search has a typo, or doesn't match any page.
So when somebody misspells your name, they might get a Google summary first… instead of your website.

Here's the ten-minute test.
Grab your phone.
Search your business name three wrong ways. Drop a letter. Swap a letter. Spell it how it sounds.
Write down what Google shows you each time.

If it's not you, add that common misspelling to your website and your Google profile description.

Try it, and tell me in the comments what Google showed you.
scripts.caption:
Spell your business name wrong on Google. Your customers will.

Search Engine Roundtable reported on Oct 12 that Google's AI Overviews often appear when a search has a typo or matches no pages. A customer who misspells your name may see a Google summary before your website.

The 10-minute test:
1. Search your business name 3 wrong ways on your phone.
2. Write down what Google shows each time.
3. If it isn't you, add the common misspelling to your website and your Google profile description.

Tell me in the comments what Google showed you.

scripts.title: Can Google read your page?
scripts.note: 3 likes, 72 views (Oct 15 card). Mime trying to highlight text on your phone on 'try to highlight the words'.
scripts.source: IG card 2026-10-15 https://www.instagram.com/p/DeiW2-CHP_K/ · Search Engine Land, Oct 13 2026
scripts.script:
Your prices are on your website.
But can Google actually read them?

Search Engine Land made the case that content locked behind a form holds a business back in AI search. The crawler reads your headline… and never reaches the facts.

Small shops do the same thing by accident. The price list sits behind a quote form. The menu is a photo.

Pull up your website on your phone.
Open your prices, menu or services page.
Does it ask for your email before it shows you anything?
Now try to highlight the words. If you can't, they're probably a picture.

Move the key facts — services, prices, hours, your city — into plain text on the page.
Then search one of those facts plus your city, and see if you show up.

Stuck? DM me the link. I'll tell you what I see.
scripts.caption:
Your prices are on your website. Can Google actually read them?

Search Engine Land argued on Oct 13 that content locked behind forms holds a brand back in AI search: a crawler reads the headline and never reaches the facts. Small shops do the same thing with price lists behind quote forms and menus saved as photos.

On your phone:
1. Open your prices, menu or services page.
2. Does it ask for an email before it shows anything?
3. Try to highlight the words. If you can't, they may be a picture.
4. Put services, prices, hours and city in plain text.
5. Search one of those facts plus your city.

Stuck? DM me the link and I'll tell you what I see.

scripts.title: Google can't match what your profile doesn't say
scripts.note: 2 likes, 1 comment (Oct 13 card). Lean in on 'every business, not just restaurants'.
scripts.source: IG card 2026-10-13 https://www.instagram.com/p/DedNPsZHOo4/ · Search Engine Roundtable, Oct 13 2026
scripts.script:
Somebody nearby just searched 'gluten-free dinner near me.'
Did Google pick you?

Google Business Profile now lets restaurants tag dishes gluten-free, dairy-free, halal and kosher, on top of vegetarian and vegan. Diners see the badge right on the dish.

But here's the part that matters for every business, not just restaurants.
Google can't match what your profile doesn't say.

Open your Google profile on your phone. Tap Menu, Products, or Services.
Restaurants: tag every dish with the badges that are true. Only what's true.
Everybody else: write three services in plain words, the way a customer would search for them.
Then reload your profile and read it like a stranger would.

Send this to a restaurant owner you know.
scripts.caption:
Somebody nearby just searched "gluten-free dinner near me." Did Google pick you?

Search Engine Roundtable reported on Oct 13 that Google Business Profile now supports gluten-free, dairy-free, halal and kosher badges on menu items. Vegetarian and vegan were already there. Only tag what is true.

Not a restaurant? Same rule. Google can't match what your profile doesn't say.

1. Open your Google profile, then Menu, Products or Services.
2. Restaurants: tag each dish with the badges that are true.
3. Everyone else: write 3 services in plain words.
4. Reload and read it like a customer.

scripts.title: AI moves fast on bad info
scripts.note: Most reach of the set: 62 reach, 97 views, 1 profile visit (Sep 30 card). Slow, knowing delivery on 'it moves fast… on bad info'.
scripts.source: IG card 2026-09-30 https://www.instagram.com/p/Dd6-3TDluqX/ · Meta Newsroom, Sep 29 2026
scripts.script:
Meta has a free AI helper for small businesses.
Before you turn it on… hear me out.

It's called Muse for Small Business. You give it a goal, it connects to tools you already use — QuickBooks, Shopify, Canva, Stripe — and it drafts the work in the background.
Meta says nothing publishes, sends, or spends without your approval. Good.

Here's my take.
An AI agent works from what your accounts already say.
Wrong hours. An old service list. Messy books.
It moves fast… on bad info.

So clean up the info first.
Then pick one chore you hate. Let it draft. Approve every single one.
And keep it away from your ad budget on day one.

Send this to an owner who's about to hand AI the keys.
scripts.caption:

One move: fix your info, pick one chore you hate, let it draft, approve every one. Keep it away from your ad budget on day one.

scripts.title: If you had to close tomorrow
scripts.note: Most views of the set: 140 views, 68 reach (Oct 15 card). Tell it like a story, not a news read. Pause after 'three days'.
scripts.source: IG card 2026-10-15 https://www.instagram.com/p/DehmyD8kfAE/ · FOX5 Vegas, Oct 14 2026
scripts.script:
Eight shops in North Las Vegas lost running water for three days.

FOX5 reported that thieves cut the backflow valves at Deer Springs Town Center. No water from Saturday through Monday. One stylist estimated she lost more than a thousand dollars in canceled appointments, because licensing rules require handwashing between clients.

You can't stop a thief.
But you control how fast your customers hear the news.

So tonight, write the one sentence you'd post on your Google profile if you had to close for a day.
Save it in your phone.
And find where special hours live on your profile, before you need them.

When something breaks, you're live in two minutes… instead of customers driving to a locked door.

Send this to a friend who owns a shop.

scripts.title: Write the label before AI does
scripts.note: 51 reach, 81 views (Oct 7 card). The comment ask is the point: answer every one with a tightened line, that's the authority play.
scripts.source: IG card 2026-10-07 https://www.instagram.com/p/DeNAZI4DkDt/ · Search Engine Roundtable, Oct 6 2026
scripts.script:
ChatGPT is testing little labels on products. 'Best for beginners.' 'Best all-rounder.'
So who writes those labels?

Search Engine Roundtable reported OpenAI testing short verdicts on product results — search expert Brodie Clark spotted it. It's only a test. But it shows where shopping is headed: a quick verdict… before anybody visits your website.

My bet? Those verdicts come from the words written about your product.
'High quality' gives AI nothing to repeat.
'Easiest first pair for new runners'… that's the label, already written.

Pick your top three products or services.
Add one sentence to each page that starts with 'Best for' — name the buyer, and the reason.

Drop one of yours in the comments, and I'll tighten it up.
scripts.caption:
ChatGPT is testing "best for" labels on products. Who writes them?

Search Engine Roundtable reported on Oct 6 that OpenAI is testing short labels on product results, like "best all-rounder" and "best cushioning." Brodie Clark spotted the test. It's only a test, but it shows where shopping is heading: a quick verdict before a shopper visits your site.

My guess: those verdicts come from the words written about each product. "High quality" gives AI nothing to repeat. "Easiest first pair for new runners" already wrote the label.

Your move: add one "Best for" sentence to your top 3 product or service pages. Name the buyer and the reason.

Drop one of yours in the comments and I'll tighten it up.
